title: Sharding Key Design
lesson:
Sharding splits one large dataset across several independent database nodes so no single machine holds all the data or serves all the traffic. The most consequential decision in a sharded design is the shard key (also called the partition key): the column or set of columns whose value decides which shard a given row lives on. Every read, write, and routing decision flows through this key. Choosing it badly is expensive to undo, because changing the shard key generally means physically moving most of the rows in the system while it is still serving live traffic.

There are two common ways to map a key to a shard. Hash-based sharding applies a hash function to the key and uses the result — often through consistent hashing — to select a shard. This spreads rows and load evenly and avoids obvious hotspots, but it destroys key ordering, so a range query like 'all orders from last week' has to fan out to every shard and merge the results. Range-based sharding instead assigns each shard a contiguous span of key values. Range scans then stay on one or a few shards, but the ranges are easy to get unbalanced, and a monotonically increasing key such as a timestamp or auto-increment id sends every new write to whichever shard owns the highest range, creating a hotspot.

A good shard key has a few properties. It should have high cardinality — many distinct values — so the data can be divided finely; a boolean flag or a country code caps how many shards are actually useful and tends to produce lopsided shard sizes. It should have even access distribution so no one shard absorbs a disproportionate share of queries. And it should align with the application's query patterns: pick a key that co-locates rows that are usually read together, such as tenant_id in a multi-tenant product or user_id for a per-user timeline, so the hot-path queries touch exactly one shard and avoid scatter-gather reads and cross-shard joins or transactions.

Even a high-cardinality key can suffer skew. The 'celebrity' or hot-key problem is when a single key — a celebrity account, a viral product — receives orders of magnitude more traffic than any other, overloading the one shard that owns it. Mitigations include adding a second dimension to the key so it splits further (a compound key like (user_id, month)), appending a bounded random suffix so a hot key is spread across N sub-partitions at the cost of reads now fanning out to those N, or giving known-hot keys their own dedicated shards. The recurring lesson is to model the real workload before committing, because resharding a live system under load is one of the most painful operations in data infrastructure.

questions.prompt: What does a table's shard key (partition key) determine?
options: Which shard a given row is stored on and how requests for it are routed
The order in which columns are displayed to the application
How many read replicas each shard is allowed to have
Which rows are cached in memory versus read from disk
questions.explanation: The shard key's value is what maps a row to a specific shard, so every read, write, and routing decision depends on it.

questions.prompt: Hash-based sharding keeps rows in sorted key order, so cross-shard range queries stay efficient.
questions.explanation: Hashing the key deliberately scrambles ordering to spread load evenly, which means a range query has to fan out to every shard.

questions.prompt: Under range-based sharding, a monotonically increasing key such as a timestamp sends every new write to a single shard, creating a ____.
questions.explanation: Because new keys always fall in the highest range, all recent writes concentrate on the shard that owns that range instead of spreading out.

questions.prompt: Why is a low-cardinality column (for example a boolean flag) a poor shard key?
options: It has too few distinct values to divide the data finely, so shards end up few and lopsided
It changes too often, forcing constant row migration between shards
It cannot be indexed, so lookups require a full scan on every shard
It is always stored uncompressed, wasting disk space
questions.explanation: With only a handful of distinct values there is no way to split the data into many balanced shards, so the partitioning is coarse and uneven.

questions.prompt: One key belongs to a celebrity account and its shard is overloaded while the others are idle. Which mitigation directly addresses this?
options: Switch every query to eventual consistency so reads can hit any shard
Append a bounded random suffix to that key so its rows spread across several sub-partitions
Add more read replicas to every shard in the cluster equally
Increase the page size of the underlying storage engine
questions.explanation: Splitting the hot key across N sub-partitions with a suffix spreads its load over multiple shards, at the cost of reads for that key now fanning out to those N.

questions.prompt: Picking a shard key that co-locates rows commonly read together (like tenant_id) helps avoid scatter-gather reads and cross-shard joins on the hot path.
questions.explanation: If the rows a query needs all live on one shard, that query hits a single node instead of fanning out and merging results from many.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a router takes to serve a point read in a hash-sharded cluster, earliest first.
items: The router sends the query to the shard that owns that hash range
The router computes a hash of the row's shard key
The matching rows are returned to the client
The hash value is mapped to a specific shard
questions.explanation: The router hashes the shard key, maps that hash to a shard, forwards the query there, and returns the shard's rows to the client.
